analysis.one_liner: Exempts the first $5 million of every estate from federal estate and gift tax.
analysis.headline: The bill to shield the first $5 million of estates from federal tax died in committee without a hearing or a vote in the 106th Congress. [S5]
analysis.plain_summary: A Florida Democrat, Rep. Peter Deutsch, introduced a bill raising the estate tax exemption to $5 million per estate and indexing it to inflation. Estates below that level already paid no estate tax under the law of the time; the bill's benefit goes entirely to the largest estates. The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted, and the 106th Congress ended without a vote. [S1] [S2] [S3] [S5]
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the wealthiest estates. Under the law as it stood, the exemption was scheduled to reach $675,000 by 2000 and phase toward $1 million; a $5 million exemption plus inflation indexing would remove all federal estate tax from the largest estates and gift-tax exposure from the largest lifetime gifts. Estates below $5 million would see no change. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Raises the unified estate and gift tax credit so that the first $5 million of any estate or lifetime gift is tax-free. [S2] [S3]
Indexes the $5 million figure to inflation after 2001, so the exemption grows automatically each year. [S3]
Conforms the family-owned business exclusion to the new $5 million exemption, removing an interplay that limited its value. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and by extension all taxpayers, since revenue from the estate tax — paid only on the largest estates — would be eliminated for estates under $5 million. If the revenue were replaced, the cost would fall on other taxpayers or the deficit. The bill as introduced contained no replacement revenue. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The tax cut is concentrated at the top: estates below $5 million already owed no estate tax under the phased-in exemption schedule of the time, so the entire benefit goes to the largest estates. [S2] [S3]
The bill provides no offsetting revenue; eliminating tax on estates up to $5 million would reduce federal receipts, adding to deficits or requiring other taxes to rise. [S3]
Indexing the exemption to inflation compounds the cost over time without any future act of Congress. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a very large benefit to a narrow group — heirs of multi-million-dollar estates — at the cost of federal revenue paid for by everyone else. It offers nothing to the roughly 98 percent of estates that already fell under the existing exemption. The inflation index makes the cost grow permanently. It is a targeted tax cut for concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: Rep. Deutsch introduced the bill in September 2000, three months before the 106th Congress ended, and the House referred it to Ways and Means. The committee never took it up, no vote was ever held, and it expired when the new Congress began in January 2001. [S5]

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Deutsch (D-FL) introduced the bill on September 7, 2000. [S1] [S5]
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day; it was the bill's last action of record. [S5]
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate tax exemption stayed at the phased-in level of the time and no revenue was lost to a $5 million exemption. No interest can be said to have gained from the bill's failure; the bill simply never had a constituency strong enough to move it in the time remaining. [S5] [S4]

for.name: Rep. Peter Deutsch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means; it never moved further.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors left no voting record and no bloc to attribute the outcome to; the bill simply never moved in committee. [S4] [S5]

industries.note: Because the bill died, they remain liable for estate tax above the existing phased-in exemption. The bill would have removed all federal estate tax from estates up to $5 million, a benefit accruing only to the largest family fortunes. [S3]
